artists.biography:
Agnes Caroline Thaarup Obel (born 1981) is a Danish singer-songwriter. Her first album, Philharmonics, was released by PIAS Recordings on 4 October 2010 in Denmark, Norway, Germany and other European countries. Since February 2011, Philharmonics is certified gold.

Agnes Obel was born Agnes Caroline Thaarup Obel in 1981. Living in Copenhagen, and coming from a musician family, Agnes Obel learned piano at a very young age. Her mother used to play Bartók and Chopin at the piano. During her childhood, Agnes Obel found inspiration in Jan Johansson’s work. Johansson’s songs, European folk tunes done in a jazzy style, have influenced the young musician a lot.

She attended high school at Det frie Gymnasium and university at Roskilde University.

At the age of seven, Agnes Thaarup worked in a little band where she used to sing and play bass guitar. The group appeared in a festival and even recorded some titles.

Later, and with the help of Danish musician and producer Elton Theander, Obel founded the Copenhagen based band Sohio. After few years of collaboration, Obel debuted as a solo singer with her first album Philharmonics (2010).

Agnes Obel writes, plays, sings, records and produces all her material herself.

She is influenced by artists such as Roy Orbison, Joni Mitchell, PJ Harvey and also by the French composers Claude Debussy, Maurice Ravel and Eric Satie.

Obel lives in Berlin.

perplexity.description:
Agnes Obel's third studio album, Myopia, released in February 2020 on Deutsche Grammophon, represents a continuation of her introspective, chamber-pop aesthetic. The Danish-born, Berlin-based artist handles vocals, piano, keys, synth, and rhythmic elements throughout the record, supplemented by guest contributions from violinist John Corban and cellist Kristina Koropecki on several tracks. The album's sonic palette remains rooted in Obel's characteristic blend of minimalist arrangements and atmospheric production, maintaining the contemplative mood that has defined her work since her 2010 debut Philharmonics.

Thematically, Myopia explores psychological introspection and existential questioning, with the album's conceptual framework emerging from Obel's examination of sleep disturbance and its cultural associations with mortality anxiety. The record includes two primary singles—"Broken Sleep," a delicate, violin-driven composition, and "Island of Doom," which features prominent vocal filtering and emotionally raw verses. Beyond these vocal-centered pieces, the album incorporates three instrumental tracks—"Roscian," "Drosera," and "Parliament of Owls"—that emphasize elegance and emotional urgency.

Myopia reflects Obel's deliberately reclusive creative process, wherein she isolates herself from external influences to draw directly from introspection rather than outside inspiration. The album maintains her artistic commitment to chamber-influenced arrangements and philosophical depth, positioning it as a natural evolution within her established discography rather than a significant stylistic departure.
